      <description><p>There is no end in sight for the drivers of illegal mining, while police action appears ineffective</p><p>Cora Bailey has been encountering illegal miners ever since she first started treating injured animals in the townships around Roodepoort, west of Johannesburg, in 1991.       <description><p>Cop30 host sets out steps to break link with coal, oil and gas as it aims to move focus from negotiating to implementing</p><p>All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.</p><p>Brazil, the host of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2025/nov/25/fossil-fuel-giants-finally-in-the-crosshairs-cop30-avoids-total-failure-with-last-ditch-deal">last year’s UN climate conference</a>, set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/03/brazil-first-global-roadmap-phasing-out-fossil-fuels">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>First polls close in Indiana and Kentucky; several key states see record turnout as Americans decide the direction of Congress for remainder of Trump’s term</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2026/nov/03/midterm-elections-full-results-senate-house-governor-races">Track live results from all 50 states</a></p></li></ul><p><em>in Austin, Texas</em></p><p>Greetings from the Austin Recreation Center in Austin, Texas, where <strong>Gina Hinojosa</strong>, the Democratic candidate for governor, greeted supporters clutching “Save our schools” signs to highlight cuts to public education.
 <br>
 <strong>
  <br>No Democrat has won a Texas gubernatorial election since Ann Richards in 1990
 </strong>, but Hinojosa, running against the incumbent Republican governor Greg Abbott, insisted that “everything is different” this time.
 <br>
 <br>
 She told reporters: “For one, Greg Abbott had never seen a poll that he was losing ever before when he ran for governor. I don’t know, there’s been like 15? I mean, so many. This election is within the margin of error and it is because Greg Abbot has done so much damage to public schools.
 <br>
 <br>
 “It is because what he has done to public schools is one example of a governor doing the bidding of the moneyed interests and not the people of Texas. Datacentres are another example. There are people all across the state very angry at this governor who no longer fears the voters and voters are fighting back in this election.”
 <br>
 <br>
 Asked how critical the Latino vote will be in this campaign, Hinojosa, 52, a civil rights and labour lawyer, replied: “It’s huge. Look, we know that when Beto [O’Rourke] ran in 2018 and came so close as a Democrat to winning [a Senate race], he got 64% of the Latino vote. When I get that I win because there’s more of us in the voting population than there were then.
 <br>
 <br>
 “Latino voters are angry about what we’re all angry about. They’re angry about schools. They’re angry about this high cost economy, which is harder to make it today than it was 12 years ago before Greg Abbott. They’re angry about the corruption and they are angry about being treated less Texan, less American than everybody else.That’s why you see Latinos turning out in big numbers.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live/2026/nov/03/midterm-election-results-live-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>
